newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan "Big Bang" to speed financial shakeout.
newsitem.headline: Japan "Big Bang" to speed financial shakeout.

text.p: Japan's plan for a "Big Bang" deregulation of its financial markets by the year 2001 will accelerate a shakeout in its financial sector, and some foreign firms could join domestic rivals among the losers.
But the broad reform proposals could also give Japan a shot at reversing its financial markets' decline and put Tokyo back in the running with London and New York, some experts said.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled the proposals on Monday. It was the first time a deadline had been set for such reforms, though many -- such as an end to fixed brokerage commissions and the tearing down of barriers among the banking, securities and insurance sectors -- were already being discussed.
Some in the foreign financial community welcomed the proposals but expressed some scepticism over implementation.

"I think that the rhetoric is very positive, but when it comes to the content ... there may be a temptation to take half-baked measures," John Baldwin, general manager of Jardine Fleming Securities Ltd.'s Tokyo branch, told Reuters.
Still, Hashimoto's decision to lend his political backing to the proposals and make financial deregulation a centrepiece of his reform plans has brightened the outlook for change.
"Hashimoto, by making this announcement, is burning his bridges," Hideo Ishihara, chairman of Goldman Sachs (Japan) Ltd told Reuters. "He is making it impossible to retreat."
Hashimoto and other policy-makers appear well aware of the need to forge ahead with reform or risk Japan's financial sector falling even further behind global rivals.
Some proposals face tough opposition from sectors likely to suffer most. "It will be a bitter battle," Ishihara said.
The securities industry is expected to be hardest hit, but Japanese banks will face some blood-letting as well.
But despite the "Big Bang" label -- an echo of London's 1986 brokerage commission liberalisation -- Japan's measures will likely to be implemented piecemeal and gradually.
Gauging the fallout is tough, given the lack of details. Many legal changes will probably not be be submitted to parliament until 1998.
"There's not enough detail to be able to judge, and even if it were specific, the question is how much will and ability there will be to follow through," one expert said.
"The Finance Ministry has always been able to find back-door ways to mitigate the effects of liberalisation."

Should reforms move ahead in line with rhetoric, the result will be more and tougher competition, pushing weaker players to the wall. "Nobody really knows, but probably it will be a real hand-to-hand battle for a while," Baldwin said.
Financial mergers are definitely in the cards. "I suspect that there will be some mergers, and also some foreign banks acquiring Japanese securities companies," Ishihara said.
Some brokerage insiders said foreign and domestic houses below the top tier would be hurt by commission deregulation and would have to diversify, if they had not already, to succeed.

Some European banks have announced plans to beef up their capital market and fixed income operations. Such institutions' deep pockets could give them an advantage in the deregulated environment, some analysts said.
Some doubts remain over whether the proposed reforms will reverse the "hollowing out" of Tokyo markets, which has seen business move to less-costly and more-open markets .

"Deregulation probably makes the market much more attractive for investors, the consumer side, but in the short-term it will probably make things much more difficult for providers," one foreign analyst said.
Costs in Tokyo remain high. "We're seeing some lower costs such as in real estate, but the biggest single item -- people -- is as or more expensive than before," Baldwin said.
But others were more optimistic.

"It's an aggressive policy and if part or all of it is implemented, it is going to maintain Tokyo's position ... and stop further whittling away of its importance in the global market place," said Andrew Simmonds, chief executive in Japan of the Barclays Group.
